questions.prompt: Which question is the best starting point for analyzing an ethical problem?

options.text: What decision must be made, by whom, and on the basis of which verified facts?
Which option would receive the most approval online?
Which person sounds most confident about the situation?
Which choice would make the problem disappear from discussion?

questions.explanation: A careful analysis begins by locating the decision, agent, and evidence. Popularity, confidence, or silence do not establish what is morally required.
questions.misconception: The strongest opinion or the most visible option is the proper starting point.
questions.originality_note: Newly authored for Aralivo; not copied from a source or reviewer bank.

questions.prompt: Which combination most closely describes a moral dilemma?

options.text: Two serious moral requirements apply, each action is possible alone, and the actions cannot all be performed together.
Two preferences feel equally strong, even though neither creates a duty.
A rule is difficult to follow because the agent forgot the deadline.
A person disagrees with a policy but has no decision to make.

questions.explanation: A moral dilemma concerns conflicting moral requirements, the agent's capacity to perform each requirement separately, and the inability to fulfill them together. Preference, forgetfulness, and disagreement alone are not enough.
questions.misconception: Any emotionally difficult choice qualifies as a moral dilemma.
questions.originality_note: Newly authored for Aralivo; not copied from a source or reviewer bank.

questions.prompt: Who is the agent in an ethical case?

options.text: The person, group, or institution responsible for deciding or acting.
Every person who hears about the situation.
Only the person who may suffer the greatest consequence.
The person who first described the situation.

questions.explanation: The agent is the responsible decision-maker or actor. Stakeholders may be affected without having the authority or responsibility to make the decision.
questions.misconception: The most affected person is always the agent.
questions.originality_note: Newly authored for Aralivo; not copied from a source or reviewer bank.

questions.prompt: Why is an ethical problem not automatically a moral dilemma?

options.text: An ethical problem may have one clearly overriding duty or a responsible solution that preserves the main requirements.
Ethical problems concern only private feelings, while dilemmas concern only laws.
Dilemmas never involve uncertainty or consequences.
A problem is ethical only after a court has ruled on it.

questions.explanation: An ethical problem can be serious and uncertain without containing two non-overridden moral requirements. Evidence, a priority rule, or a third option may make one response responsible.
questions.misconception: If a choice is hard, the options must be morally balanced.
questions.originality_note: Newly authored for Aralivo; not copied from a source or reviewer bank.

questions.prompt: A university team changes a reporting procedure after discovering that students cannot safely use it. At which level is the change mainly being made?

options.text: Organizational, because a group is changing its procedure and responsibilities.
Individual, because only one person's private preference matters.
Technical, because procedures can never raise moral questions.
Purely personal, because institutions cannot be responsible.

questions.explanation: The response changes how an institution organizes reporting and protects people, so the immediate level is organizational. The underlying access pattern could also invite structural analysis.
questions.misconception: Only a one-to-one decision can be an ethical issue.

questions.prompt: Which finding most strongly suggests that an apparent two-option dilemma is false?

options.text: A protected reporting route can address the safety risk without publicizing an unverified allegation.
Both stated choices would be emotionally uncomfortable.
The decision has a deadline later in the week.
The people involved have different personal preferences.

questions.explanation: A safe, feasible third route can preserve important requirements that the original framing treated as mutually exclusive. Discomfort, deadlines, and preferences do not test the structure of the dilemma.
questions.misconception: Finding any additional idea automatically proves the original concern was trivial.

questions.prompt: Which person is a stakeholder in a campus safety decision?

options.text: A visitor who may be exposed to the unsafe demonstration.
Only the person who signed the equipment checkout form.
Only people who already agree with the coordinator.
No one, because safety is a technical matter.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder can be affected by the decision even without authority over it. A visitor's safety is relevant to the moral analysis.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to say that one moral requirement overrides another in a particular case?

options.text: The circumstances give one requirement enough priority to defeat or postpone the other for that decision.
The less important requirement has no value in any future situation.
The agent may ignore all duties once a priority is selected.
The requirement was never moral in the first place.

questions.explanation: An override is context-sensitive priority, not a declaration that the other requirement is always meaningless. It can turn a conflict into a problem with a defensible priority.
questions.misconception: Priority in one case permanently cancels a moral requirement.

questions.prompt: A student faces immediate pressure, while an inaccessible institutional form has created the repeated problem. Which analysis is most complete?

options.text: Analyze the student's immediate responsibility and the institutional design that keeps producing the barrier.
Blame the student alone because systems cannot have ethical effects.
Ignore the student because only structural patterns matter.
Treat accessibility as a preference outside ethical reasoning.

questions.explanation: Individual responsibility and structural conditions can coexist. A response should protect the person now and improve the system that creates repeated burdens.
questions.misconception: An ethical analysis must choose either individual or structural responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which fact is most useful for deciding whether a confidentiality conflict is genuine?

options.text: Whether the risk is credible, serious, foreseeable, and reportable through a limited safe channel.
Whether the secret was written in a message rather than spoken.
Whether the person who shared it is popular in the group.
Whether revealing it would make the agent feel relieved.

questions.explanation: The seriousness, credibility, foreseeability, and available reporting safeguards determine whether limited disclosure may be justified. Format, popularity, and emotional relief do not settle the conflict.
questions.misconception: Confidentiality is either absolute or irrelevant, with no need to examine context.

questions.prompt: Why should an agent separate verified facts from assumptions before selecting an action?

options.text: An assumption can create a conflict or remove an option that the actual evidence would change.
Facts are useful only in scientific subjects, not in ethics.
Assumptions are always morally wrong regardless of their source.
Verified facts guarantee that reasonable people will choose identically.

questions.explanation: Incomplete or inaccurate information can make the choice appear narrower or more urgent than it is. Facts improve the reasoning without guaranteeing one universal response.
questions.misconception: Ethical judgment is only about values and never about evidence.

questions.prompt: Which action best demonstrates responsible follow-through after a difficult ethical decision?

options.text: Document the reasons, communicate necessary information, reduce avoidable harm, and review the result.
Stop thinking about the case as soon as a decision is announced.
Hide the trade-off so affected people do not ask questions.
Treat regret as proof that the decision must be reversed immediately.

questions.explanation: Ethical responsibility includes mitigation, transparent reasons, and later review. Avoidance, concealment, or an automatic reversal does not provide a reliable process.
questions.misconception: Ethical responsibility ends when the first choice is made.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply; more than one answer may be selected. Which actions help test whether an apparent dilemma is false?

options.text: Search for a safe third option or a way to sequence the actions.
Check whether one requirement clearly overrides the other in context.
Verify an assumption that made the options seem incompatible.
Choose the option that produces the most dramatic story.
Ask whether a qualified authority can share responsibility safely.

questions.explanation: Alternative search, priority testing, fact verification, and safe consultation can reveal that the apparent conflict is avoidable or narrower than first stated. Drama is not a test.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply; more than one answer may be selected. Which steps can make a response more responsible when a hard choice remains?

options.text: Use the least intrusive action that adequately addresses the risk.
Tell affected people the information they need while protecting unnecessary private details.
Record the reasons, uncertainty, safeguards, and review plan.
Promise that no one will experience a cost.
Plan repair if the process caused preventable harm.

questions.explanation: Proportion, necessary communication, documentation, and repair make decisions more accountable. A promise of zero cost is usually impossible and can mislead affected people.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply; more than one answer may be selected. Which questions are useful after a decision leaves moral residue?

options.text: Was the process fair and were the relevant facts adequate?
Which value or relationship was sacrificed and how can it be acknowledged?
What safeguard or policy change could reduce the same burden later?
Can regret be used by itself as proof that the decision was wrong?
Is explanation, apology, restitution, or support appropriate and safe?

questions.explanation: Moral residue invites review, recognition, repair, and prevention. Regret is evidence of a cost or concern, but it is not by itself a complete verdict.
